title: She called it a noble letter.
subtitle: Bilqis gathers her chiefs
then: Bilqis was amazed and confused when the letter landed in her chamber. Ibn Kathir says she called it noble {idea}because of the wondrous way it came: a bird delivered it, then stood aside out of good manners.{/idea} She gathered her commanders, ministers and leaders.
now: A message arrives that could hurt your pride: a note from your landlord, a hard email from your manager. {idea}You can see what is honorable in it before you react.{/idea} Bilqis did not tear it up. She called people in to think.
old: A message that challenges me is an attack to push back on.
new: A challenging message can be noble, and deserves to be read with care.
try: Reread one hard message you received recently, looking for what is fair in it.

title: The letter began with the name of the Merciful.
subtitle: How a prophet opened a hard message
then: The queen read the letter aloud. It named its sender, Sulayman, and began {idea}In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says they knew then it was from Allah's Prophet and that {trap}they could not match him.{/trap}
now: You are about to write the difficult text: to an ex, to a sibling you fell out with, to the client who has not paid. {idea}What you put first sets the tone.{/idea} Sulayman, with all his power, opened with mercy.
old: When I have the upper hand, I can lead with strength.
new: Even a firm message starts best with Allah's name and His mercy.
try: Say Bismillah before the next hard message you write today, and let it soften one word.

title: Do not be arrogant. Come in submission.
subtitle: A short letter, straight to the point
then: Ibn Kathir says the letter was {idea}the utmost in brevity and eloquence, coming straight to the point.{/idea} Qatadah explained: do not be arrogant with me. Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said: {trap}do not refuse or be too arrogant to come.{/trap}
now: You write five paragraphs to say one thing, and the point gets lost. {idea}Two clear lines can do more than a long speech.{/idea} And the heart of the matter is often the same: let go of pride and come back.
new: The clearest call is short: drop the pride and turn to Allah.
try: Rewrite one message you need to send in two sentences.

title: A queen who would not decide alone.
subtitle: Bilqis asks her chiefs for advice
then: After reading Sulayman's letter, Bilqis consulted her leaders. She said she would {idea}decide no case until they came together and offered their advice.{/idea} The surah introduction describes her as a ruler of a wealthy people who still did not act from vanity.
now: The big decision: moving cities, a new job, a marriage proposal. {idea}You do not have to decide it alone in your head at 2am.{/idea} Call the people whose judgment you trust and ask.
old: Asking for advice makes me look weak or unsure.
new: Even someone with full authority is wiser when she listens first.
try: Ask one trusted person for their honest view on a decision you are facing.

title: We are strong, they said, but you decide.
subtitle: The chiefs offer force, then defer
then: Ibn Kathir explains the chiefs {trap}reminded her of their great numbers, preparedness and strength{/trap}, then handed the decision back. Their words: {idea}we have the power if you want to fight, but the matter is yours to decide.{/idea}
now: Your friends are ready to fight your battle: we will tell him off, we will post about it. {trap}Being able to hit back is not a reason to.{/trap} The best advice leaves room for you to think it over.
old: If I have the strength to win a fight, I should use it.
new: Strength is a tool, and the wiser question is what will actually help.
try: In one disagreement today, choose not to use an advantage you have.

title: She knew what conquering kings leave behind.
subtitle: Bilqis weighs the cost of war
then: Ibn Abbas explained that Bilqis said kings {trap}destroy a town they enter and make its most honorable people the lowest.{/trap} Then Allah said: {idea}and thus they do{/idea}, confirming her words. She saw where a fight would lead.
now: You picture winning the argument with your spouse, the lawsuit with your neighbor. {trap}Winning can still wreck the house.{/trap} Bilqis looked past the victory to what it would leave behind.
old: Winning a conflict is the same as coming out well.
new: Before any fight, I should picture what it will do to the people around me.
try: Before your next argument, ask what the relationship will look like afterward.

title: She chose a gift and patience over a fight.
subtitle: Testing whether he was a king or a prophet
then: Bilqis turned to {idea}peaceful means, seeking a truce.{/idea} Qatadah praised her wisdom: she understood how gift-giving has a good effect on people. Ibn Abbas and others said she reasoned: {idea}if he accepts it he is a king; if not, he is a Prophet, so follow him.{/idea}
now: The tension with your in-laws is building. You could text something sharp, or you could bring dessert on Friday and see. {reward}A gift and a pause can tell you more than a fight.{/reward}
old: When someone pressures me, I must either fight or give in.
new: A gift and patience can lower tension and reveal what someone really wants.
try: Give a small gift to someone you are tense with this week.

title: What Allah gave me is better than your gift.
subtitle: Sulayman refuses to be bought
then: Scholars said she sent {reward}a huge gift of gold, jewels and pearls.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says Sulayman did not even look at it. He asked if they were trying {trap}to flatter him with wealth so he would leave them with their shirk{/trap}, and said what Allah gave him was better.
now: Someone offers you a bonus to look the other way. A friend's family offers money so you will drop a complaint. {idea}When you are content with what Allah gave you, you cannot be bought.{/idea}
old: If the offer is big enough, it is fine to bend a little.
new: What Allah has given me is enough, so no gift should buy my silence about what is right.
try: Name one thing someone could offer you to compromise. Decide now that it is not for sale.

title: Send the gift back. The message stands.
subtitle: A firm reply that led to her submission
then: Sulayman sent the envoys back with their gift and a firm warning. Ibn Kathir says when they reported it, {reward}she and her people paid heed and came to him in humility, intending to follow him in Islam.{/reward} When Sulayman realized they were coming, {reward}he rejoiced greatly.{/reward}
now: You returned the expensive present because it came with strings. It felt harsh. {idea}A clear no can be what finally lets the other person take you seriously.{/idea} The goal is not to win but to see them come round.
old: Refusing a gift will only make things worse.
new: A firm, clear no can open the door, and the hope behind it is the other person's good.
try: Give one clear, kind no today that you have been avoiding.

title: Who can bring her throne before she arrives?
subtitle: Sulayman prepares a sign for the queen
then: Yazid bin Ruman reported that Bilqis said she knew he was more than a king. She locked her throne in the innermost of seven rooms and set out. Ibn Kathir says Sulayman wanted it brought {idea}to furnish proof of his prophethood before Bilqis and her people.{/idea}
now: Your cousin is coming to visit, curious but unsure about faith. {idea}What you prepare before they arrive matters.{/idea} Not to impress them with yourself, but to help them see something true.
old: When I want someone to take my faith seriously, I should talk more.
new: I can prepare signs ahead of time, through how I live, that point beyond me.
try: Before seeing someone today, plan one kind act that reflects your faith without words.

title: Strong and trustworthy, but not fast enough.
subtitle: The Ifrit's offer
then: Mujahid said the Ifrit was a giant jinn. He offered to bring the throne before Sulayman rose from his sitting, which As-Suddi said lasted until noon. Ibn Abbas explained his claim: {idea}strong enough to carry it and trustworthy with the jewels it contains.{/idea}
now: You are hiring someone, or choosing who to leave your kids with. Skill is half of it. {idea}Can they carry it, and will they keep it safe?{/idea} You want to be both of those for the people who depend on you.
old: Being good at the job is all that counts.
new: Real competence is strength and trustworthiness together.
try: Do one task today with both full effort and complete honesty.

title: The throne arrived, and he called it a test.
subtitle: Gratitude benefits the grateful
then: Ibn Abbas said the man was Asif, Sulayman's scribe. He prayed, and the throne appeared in a blink. Sulayman said {idea}this is by the grace of my Lord, to test whether I am grateful.{/idea} Ibn Kathir adds: Allah has no need of anyone's worship, and gratitude is for the grateful.
now: The thing you prayed for arrives faster than you hoped: the visa, the test result, the offer letter. {idea}That moment is the exam, not the reward.{/idea} Do you say al-hamdu lillah, or just move on to the next thing?
old: When I get what I asked for, the test is over.
new: Getting what I wanted is itself the test, and thanks helps me, not Allah.
try: Recall the last prayer that was answered. Thank Allah for it specifically today.

title: Change her throne a little and see.
subtitle: A test of her judgment
then: Sulayman ordered the throne altered. Mujahid said red was made yellow and green made red. Ibn Kathir explains it was to see {idea}whether she recognized it and how composed she would be{/idea}, and whether she would be guided.
now: Life rearranges the familiar: a parent ages, a job changes shape, your city looks different. {idea}Can you still see clearly when things are rearranged?{/idea} That is often the real test.
old: Tests are about catching me out.
new: Many tests are about whether I see clearly when the familiar looks different.
try: Look at one changed situation in your life and name what is still the same underneath.

title: As though it were the very same.
subtitle: Her careful answer about the throne
then: Ibn Kathir calls her {idea}wise and steadfast, intelligent and strong-willed.{/idea} She did not rush to say yes, since her throne was far away, nor no, since it resembled hers. Her answer was {idea}the ultimate in intelligence and resolve.{/idea} Mujahid said Sulayman then spoke of the knowledge given to them.
now: Someone asks you about a rumor, a diagnosis, a story you only half know. You feel pressure to be sure. {idea}Saying exactly what you know, no more, no less, is a skill.{/idea}
old: I need to give a firm yes or no to look smart.
new: An honest answer can be careful and match exactly what I know.
try: Today, when unsure, say "I think so, but I am not certain" instead of guessing.

title: Her old worship was what held her back.
subtitle: What stood between Bilqis and the truth
then: Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr read this as Sulayman's words: {trap}what stopped her from worshipping Allah alone was what she used to worship{/trap}, because she came from a disbelieving people. Ibn Kathir notes she declared her Islam soon after.
now: You are smart, educated, thoughtful. And still some habits stick because "this is how our family does it." {trap}Brilliance does not free you from what you grew up around.{/trap} Noticing it is the first step.
old: Clever people are not held back by habits they inherited.
new: Even a sharp mind can be held back by what it was raised to bow to.
try: Name one habit you keep only because your surroundings do. Ask if it pleases Allah.

title: I wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman.
subtitle: The glass floor and her turning

row.title: I submit
sub: to the Lord of the worlds

then: Sulayman had a palace of smooth glass built over flowing water. Bilqis thought it was water. Ibn Kathir says when she saw what Allah had given him, {reward}she submitted and said she had wronged herself{/reward} by worshipping the sun, and she submitted {idea}together with Sulayman to Allah.{/idea}
now: You spent years sure you had something figured out, then one moment shows you were wrong. {reward}"I wronged myself" is not defeat.{/reward} And you do not turn to a person. You stand beside them, before Allah.
old: Admitting I was wrong means losing to someone.
new: Admitting I wronged myself is how I join others in turning to Allah.
try: Say "I was wrong about this" to Allah, out loud, about one thing today.
